newsitem.title: GERMANY: German court awards RWE partial damages.
newsitem.headline: German court awards RWE partial damages.

text.p: German diversified utility RWE AG is entitled to partial damages from the state of Rheinland Palatinate over delays to the operation of a nuclear power plant, the Federal Supreme Court ruled on Thursday.
RWE had demanded seven billion marks in damages for its initial investment, lost profits and cost of maintaining the station at Muelheim Kaerlich, near Koblenz in western Germany.
The court ruled that RWE must be compensated for the building and financing costs of the plant as well as the stoppage of business, but not for the full time of the hold-up.
But the court said RWE did not have to be compensated for lost profits. The exact level of damages is to be set by a court in Koblenz.
The decision means that German states could now be faced by a flood of regressive claims for damages for other large-scale projects held up, or halted by the legal approval process.
Shares in RWE rose to touch a high of 70 marks after the decision, up 1.60 marks, or 2.3 percent, but then slipped back to trade around 69 marks.
One dealer said that the hopes for damages in the billions of marks for RWE would probably not be fulfilled.
The building of the plant was authorised in 1975, when Chancellor Helmut Kohl was premier of the state.
But in 1988, after less than a year of trial operations, the 1,300 megawatt plant was forced to shut down, because of a mistake in the original authorisation.
It has stood idle ever since and RWE said the cost of maintaining the plant has been 200 million marks each year.

A change in one of the reactor buildings to make it more safe in case of earthquakes was not included in the original plans and in 1988 the state decided this meant the original authorisation had been wrong.

"It's a German speciality to hold up authorisation in such a legal jungle," said Manfred Petroll, spokesman for the German Atom Forum, a group which provides information on the peaceful use of nuclear energy.
"The paradox is the plant has been held up because it made changes that were better for safety," said Petroll.
But in 1995 the high administrative court in Koblenz ruled that a new authorisation did still not take earthquake danger sufficiently into account.

The legal battle over the plant is still not over. Last week the Federal administrative court in Berlin said a revision of the original authorisation should be allowed, meaning that the plant could finally come on stream.
Community activists campaigning against the plant criticised this decision and said the plant, now in its third decade, was too old to be put into operation.
Muelheim-Kaerlich is the second RWE reactor to fall foul of legal and political wrangling.
Another nuclear plant, at Kalkar, near the Dutch border, was closed down in 1991 and is now the site of a planned amusement park.
The plant, which cost seven billion marks to build but never generated a watt of electricity for consumers, was the focus of anti-nuclear protests in the 1980s.
